blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights two papers from the 'Re-coding Black Mirror' workshop at WWW'18, both inspired by the Black Mirror episode 'Be Right Back.' The first paper, 'The rise of emotion-aware conversational agents' by Mensio et al., explores the technical feasibility and ethical implications of creating AI systems that mimic human emotions and personalities using text, voice, and embodied robotics. The author notes the progress in affective computing and generative conversational agents, citing real-world examples like Replika.ai and Lyrebird, while also raising concerns about addiction, social withdrawal, and the erosion of human relationships. The second paper, 'Digital Zombies - the reanimation of our digital selves' by Tietz et al., examines the ethical and legal challenges of posthumous digital avatars, questioning ownership, consent, and exploitation of deceased individuals' data. The blog emphasizes the societal risks of unchecked technological advancements, mirroring themes from Black Mirror, and underscores the need for careful consideration of human values in AI development.
paper_title: The rise of emotion-aware conversational agents
paper_abstract: A future where the conversation with machines can potentially involve mutual emotions between the parties may be not so far in time. Inspired by the episode of Black Mirror “Be Right Back” and Replika, a futuristic app that promises to be “your best friend”, in this work we are considering the positive and negative points of including an automated learning conversational agent inside the personal world of feelings and emotions. These systems can impact both single individuals and society, worsening an already critical situation. Our conclusion is that a regulation on the artificial emotional content should be considered before actually going beyond some one-way-only limits.
